models.name: Model-Lumen-RANS (MLR)
models.what_it_computes: Steady incompressible RANS of the catheter’s internal lumen and side ports to predict pressure drop versus flow, wall shear stress, and entrance/exit loss coefficients under prescribed flow rates.

models.name: Model-Nav-NarrowGap (MNNG)
models.what_it_computes: Transient CFD in the pericatheter narrow gap using lubrication approximations within tortuous vessel geometries to estimate hydrodynamic drag during advancement, near-wall shear at contact, and pressure fields influencing trackability.

mechanisms.name: Tortuous-path bending and torsion during navigation
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Resistance to advancement and steering through compound curvatures drives the push force required and the risk of buckling or loss of tip control (trackability).

mechanisms.name: Guidewire–catheter sliding friction within the distal lumen
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Friction along the wire–lumen interface modulates deliverability and can dominate incremental push force in tight anatomies (trackability).

mechanisms.name: Lumen viscous pressure drop under steady infusion
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Viscous losses set the flow resistance and affect achievable infusion rates and upstream pump pressures (flow resistance).

mechanisms.name: Entrance/exit losses and side-hole mixing under pulsatile delivery
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Unsteady local losses and port interactions add to mean pressure drop and influence jet patterns relevant to hemolysis and drug dispersion (flow resistance).

deviation.detail: All credibility factor scores are reported on a 0–12 numeric scale defined for this study (0 = no credible evidence; 12 = compelling, decision-grade evidence).

findings.mechanism: Lumen viscous pressure drop under steady infusion
spans: MLR predictions of total pressure drop achieved a mean absolute percent error (MAPE) of 3.1% across 96 operating points, with a maximum absolute error of 7.2% at 200 mL/min for the 0.018 in. lumen with 0.018 in. wire (expected near-annular flow).

The predicted decomposition into viscous and entrance losses aligned with measured changes upon altering entrance geometry (adding a radiused funnel reduced drop by 10–12% experimentally; MLR predicted 11–13%).
findings.span: MLR predictions of total pressure drop achieved a mean absolute percent error (MAPE) of 3.1% across 96 operating points, with a maximum absolute error of 7.2% at 200 mL/min for the 0.018 in. lumen with 0.018 in. wire (expected near-annular flow).

spans: MLR predicted cycle-averaged loss coefficients with MAPE 6.5% across 24 configurations and captured the modest increase (3–5%) in mean drop associated with out-of-phase side-port jets.
Peak wall shear near ports was within 12% of particle image velocimetry (PIV) estimates in an acrylic surrogate (n = 3 tests).

findings.factor: Relevance of the quantities of interest
spans: For pulsatile delivery, cycle-averaged loss coefficients are compared to steady-flow equivalents used in verification to justify the use of steady surrogates or to quantify additional headroom.

MLR’s predicted mean increase in loss coefficient under 1 Hz sinusoidal flow (3–5% above steady for the tested geometries) provides the basis for applying a correction factor in acceptance calculations when pulsatility is expected.

findings.mechanism: Tortuous-path bending and torsion during navigation
spans: Advancement speeds of 5, 10, and 20 mm/s were imposed in tests and simulations.

Gap thickness h(s,θ) was constructed from nominal OD and jig ID with measured jig diameters (precision-bored PTFE tubes) and temperature-corrected polymer shaft diameters; the resulting mean gap in non-contact sections ranged 25–125 µm with estimated SD 8–20 µm across manufacturing lots.
findings.span: Advancement speeds of 5, 10, and 20 mm/s were imposed in tests and simulations.

findings.mechanism: Tortuous-path bending and torsion during navigation
spans: For MNNG, axial grid refinement with ∆s of 1.0, 0.5, and 0.25 mm yielded changes in integrated hydrodynamic drag of 0.8–1.3% for coronary paths and 0.5–0.9% for peripheral paths at 10 mm/s advancement.
Convergence tolerances on the nonlinear pressure–conductance iterations were tightened from 105 to 106 with negligible change (<0.1%) to integrated outputs, confirming iteration adequacy.
findings.span: For MNNG, axial grid refinement with ∆s of 1.0, 0.5, and 0.25 mm yielded changes in integrated hydrodynamic drag of 0.8–1.3% for coronary paths and 0.5–0.9% for peripheral paths at 10 mm/s advancement.

findings.mechanism: Tortuous-path bending and torsion during navigation
spans: Across all paths and three catheter OD variants (0.028, 0.032, 0.038 in.), MNNG predicted the hydrodynamic drag with MAPE 7.9% (n = 60 path–device combinations), with higher discrepancies (up to 12%) in the most tortuous coronary path where intermittent contact patches caused variability.
Bias was 1.8% (model slightly conservative).

The model captured the expected scaling with viscosity (drag increased by 13–15% when viscosity was raised from 3.0 to 3.5 mPa·s, vs 12–16% measured) and gap (drag decreased by 22–26% when OD was reduced by 0.004 in., vs 20–25% measured).
findings.span: Across all paths and three catheter OD variants (0.028, 0.032, 0.038 in.), MNNG predicted the hydrodynamic drag with MAPE 7.9% (n = 60 path–device combinations), with higher discrepancies (up to 12%) in the most tortuous coronary path where intermittent contact patches caused variability.
